title: Rest at home
hookLine: Martha serves, Mary sits: a home that lets you rest, and the old debate over which sister was right
tomorrow: three strangers in the heat of the day. why did an old man run?

lines: ONE PERSON DOING ALL OF IT.
cards: A guest is coming, the kitchen is chaos, and one person is doing all of it. Luke's Gospel has that scene. Jesus comes to the house of two sisters.
Martha is busy with all the serving. Her sister Mary sits at his feet and listens. Martha comes to him: doesn't it bother you that my sister has left me to serve alone?

The answer, in the King James words: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."

teach.b: Readers have argued about it, and Martha's side deserves its best case. Someone has to cook. Welcoming a guest is holy work, and Martha is the one doing it.

The medieval preacher Meister Eckhart took her side in a sermon on this very passage: he praised Martha as the one who had learned to stay close to God in the middle of work, while Mary, he suggested, was still learning.

teach.h: MARY: THE LISTENING THAT COMES FIRST.
teach.b: Other readers made Mary the picture of the contemplative life: the listening that comes first. Now notice what Jesus doesn't say. He doesn't call the serving bad.
He says Martha is careful and troubled about many things, and that one thing is needful.

teach.h: THE TROUBLE IS THE MANY, NOT THE WORK.
teach.b: The trouble is the many, not the work. That's a teaching Christians draw from the scene: make room to sit and listen, even in a busy house, because rest doesn't come from the list being finished.
It comes from turning, for a while, to the one thing.
A home can help with that: one chair, one corner, where nothing asks you to serve.

how: Christians read the Martha and Mary story as a call to make time for prayer and listening, and some keep a chair or corner at home set aside for it.

o: a vacation away from the house and all its chores
sleeping in late every weekend to recover
a place where you can stop and simply be, at home

games.q: two sisters, one house: tap the pairs.
p: sat at his feet and listened

s: Jesus tells Martha that serving is wrong
he says she's careful and troubled about many things. he never calls the serving bad.
some readers have taken Martha's side
the preacher Meister Eckhart praised her in a sermon on this passage.

games.q: your book group splits: half say Martha is the real hero, half say Mary. you're asked for the Martha side's best case. what is it?
o: welcoming a guest is holy work too, and someone had to do it.
Mary was lazy, and Jesus only defended her to be polite.
Jesus later changed his mind and told Mary to help.
games.why: Martha's case is the work of welcome, and Eckhart praised her. Luke's Jesus still says Mary chose the good part; the trouble is the many things.

practice: Look around the room you're in and find one spot that could be a resting corner: a chair, a step, a patch of floor by a window. Move there if you can, or simply look at it. Then let the many things wait while you sit.

wordCard.voice: Rest at home: a place where the many things wait and the one thing gets your attention. Mary's place at his feet.

orig.note: Greek: the good part, what Luke says Mary chose.

carryVoice: Keep this close: a restful corner, where Martha's real work gets set down for a while. Day 1718, done.
